name: Revenue Analytics
goal: Report revenue the way a CFO defends it — net of returns, at the right grain, with subtotals that tie out.

brief.body: Investors don't care about gross revenue — they care about quality of revenue. The first question on every number will be 'is that net of returns?' I need revenue and margin by category and quarter I'd be comfortable putting on a slide. And while you're in there — tell me whether our discounting is buying us anything or just torching margin.

clinic.title: Aggregation that survives scrutiny
clinic.body: Conditional aggregation computes gross, net, counts and rates in one pass. HAVING filters groups. GROUP BY ROLLUP(a,b) adds subtotals + a grand total, and GROUPING() labels those total rows. Every division gets NULLIF(denominator,0). Carry-over: use customers_clean anywhere you touch customers — never the raw table.

classwork.title: Return-adjusted revenue by category & quarter

steps.instr: Get the grain right first: one row per (category, year-quarter).
steps.sql:
SELECT Category, OrderYear, OrderQuarter, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY Category, OrderYear, OrderQuarter
ORDER BY Category, OrderYear, OrderQuarter;
steps.checkpoint: 8 categories x up to 12 quarters ~ up to 96 rows. Use orders.Category directly — no join to products (which would drop deprecated-SKU revenue).

steps.instr: Layer in gross, net & lost-to-returns. (Note: OrderQuarter is already stored as 'Q1-2022' etc., so use it directly as the period label.)
steps.sql:
SELECT Category,
  OrderQuarter AS period,
  COUNT(*) AS orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS returned_orders,
  ROUND(SUM(Revenue), 0) AS gross_revenue,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE Revenue END),0) AS net_revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY Category, OrderYear, OrderQuarter
ORDER BY Category, OrderYear, OrderQuarter;
steps.checkpoint: net_revenue <= gross_revenue in every row. Returns are zeroed, not deleted.

classwork.reference:
SELECT Category,
  OrderQuarter AS period,
  COUNT(*) AS orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS returned_orders,
  ROUND(SUM(Revenue), 0) AS gross_revenue,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE Revenue END),0) AS net_revenue,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE GrossProfit END),0) AS net_profit,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE GrossProfit END)
        / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE Revenue END), 0) * 100, 2) AS net_margin_pct
FROM orders
GROUP BY Category, OrderYear, OrderQuarter
ORDER BY Category, OrderYear, OrderQuarter;

tickets.title: Is our discounting profitable? Margin by discount band
tickets.prompt: Bucket orders into discount bands and show, per band, volume, revenue, gross profit and margin %. Exclude returns and non-positive revenue. Output exactly these five columns in this order: discount_band, orders, revenue (rounded to 0), gross_profit (rounded to 0), margin_pct (rounded to 2). Bands must be in logical order (0%, 1-10%, 11-20%, 21-30%, 30%+), not alphabetical.
acceptanceCriteria: Returns & non-positive revenue excluded (WHERE ReturnFlag='No' AND Revenue>0)
revenue & gross_profit rounded to 0; margin_pct rounded to 2
Then answer for yourself: which band turns margin negative?
hints: CASE on Discount_Pct for the bands.
ORDER BY MIN(Discount_Pct) forces logical band order.
tickets.selfCheck: The auto-grader checks the table. The business answer (where margin turns negative) is yours to state — it's the '30%+' band, which sells below cost.

tickets.title: Category x Region net revenue matrix with subtotals
tickets.prompt: Net revenue by category and region in one table, with per-category subtotals and a grand total — board-deck style. Remember NULL regions exist (handled as 'Unknown' in customers_clean).
acceptanceCriteria: Uses ROLLUP for subtotals + grand total
Total rows clearly labelled (not blank cells)
hints: Label totals with CASE WHEN GROUPING(col)=1 THEN 'ALL …'.
ORDER BY GROUPING(...) keeps subtotals beneath their detail rows.
tickets.solution:
SELECT
  CASE WHEN GROUPING(o.Category)=1 THEN 'ALL CATEGORIES' ELSE o.Category END AS category,
  CASE WHEN GROUPING(c.Region)=1 THEN 'ALL REGIONS' ELSE c.Region END AS region,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN o.ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 0 ELSE o.Revenue END), 0) AS net_revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers_clean c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY ROLLUP (o.Category, c.Region)
ORDER BY GROUPING(o.Category), o.Category, GROUPING(c.Region), c.Region;
tickets.modelNote: GROUPING() = 1 on subtotal/total rows is how you label them instead of leaving NULLs. DuckDB supports ROLLUP and GROUPING() just like Databricks.

tickets.title: Return-rate hotspots putting revenue at risk
tickets.prompt: Find subcategories whose return rate is more than 2x their own category's average, and quantify revenue exposed. Needs SubCategory (from products) — so mind the deprecated-SKU rows, and document your join choice.
acceptanceCriteria: Return rate per subcategory vs its category average
Revenue at risk quantified per hotspot
One-line written justification of the join choice
hints: Two CTEs: per-subcategory stats, then per-category average.
INNER JOIN products here — a row with no known subcategory can't be bucketed (and that exclusion is itself a finding to report separately).
tickets.solution:
WITH by_sub AS (
  SELECT p.Category, p.SubCategory, COUNT(*) AS orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS returns,
    ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN o.ReturnFlag='Yes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)*100.0/COUNT(*),2) AS ret_rate,
    ROUND(SUM(o.Revenue),0) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN products p ON o.ProductID = p.ProductID
  GROUP BY p.Category, p.SubCategory
),
cat_avg AS (
  SELECT Category, ROUND(SUM(returns)*100.0/SUM(orders),2) AS cat_ret_rate FROM by_sub GROUP BY Category
)
SELECT b.Category, b.SubCategory, b.orders, b.ret_rate, a.cat_ret_rate, b.revenue AS revenue_at_risk
FROM by_sub b JOIN cat_avg a ON b.Category=a.Category
WHERE b.ret_rate > 2*a.cat_ret_rate
ORDER BY revenue_at_risk DESC;
tickets.modelNote: Join justification: INNER JOIN is right because rows without a known subcategory can't be bucketed — but report the ₹ on deprecated SKUs separately so leadership knows what's excluded. The dropped rows are themselves a finding.
